warnings.text: Your 6 spa jets + gas heater peak (~90 GPM) is a little over the ~84 GPM that 2″ return plumbing carries at the recommended velocity. That's fine for short feature runs, but expect some extra noise and energy at full speed.

Heads up on the salt cell: its flow switch trips on water velocity, so a 2″ tee needs roughly 25 GPM. The top pick can idle near 12 GPM, which is below that — set your lowest speed high enough to close the switch, or the cell will quietly stop making chlorine.

warnings.text: Some models have disputed published output (badged below). Measured output generally matches published figures, so no derating is applied — but confirm with the manufacturer.

If you run a variable-speed pump, keep the lowest speed above roughly 25 GPM (2″ tee). The flow switch reacts to water velocity, so too slow a speed stops chlorine production without any obvious fault.

Hold CYA at 70–80 once you are running on salt. Higher CYA shields chlorine from sunlight, so the cell makes less to hold the same FC and lasts longer. Note the output percentage is a share of pump run time — change your schedule and you will need to re-tune it.

Cell life is measured in generating hours — roughly 10,000 for OEM cells, nearer 7,000 for generics (some offshore cells as low as 3,000). At about 94% output the top pick spends most of the day idle, which is exactly why TFP says to oversize.

Top pick needs about 94% output at 8h/day. Running the pump roughly 17h/day at low RPM would drop it to about 45% — usually cheaper than buying a larger cell, keeps scale down, and the cell lasts longer when it works less hard.

Chlorine demand is estimated at 3 ppm/day for your climate. If you track your daily FC loss (an overnight FC loss test, or your PoolMath logs), entering it makes the output percentages specific to your pool.

Plumb in a heater bypass while you are at it. Isolate a leaking or failed heater without shutting the pump down, so the pool keeps circulating and chlorinating. It also protect the copper heat exchanger when pH drops below about 7.0 — acidic water erodes the core and can stain the pool. And it cut back pressure for the ~95% of the time the heater is not in use; heat pumps restrict more than gas heaters because of smaller internal piping.

Before you buy: check the warranty. Internet purchases and owner installation can void coverage on some brands, a few require a certified installer, and most require product registration. Bundled purchases with professional install sometimes carry a longer warranty.
